13398-the-evolution-of-dodd-a-pedagogica:
William Hawley Smith's 1897 pedagogical story follows Dodd Weaver from a joyful birth in the Weaver household through school struggles for the survival of the fittest. Dodd learns, argues, and tests teachers, once turning a question about leaning against a tree back on Amos, who waves a slat and demands an answer.

Mr. Bright, his teacher, dashes out Dodd's shameful oaths in a composition and insists on rights bound to respect, leaving the schoolroom in consternation as Dodd stands pale with anger at the door. Smith uses one boy's chances and changes to argue that schools exist for the child, not the child for schools, and that character grows through trial.
21660-an-introduction-to-the-industrial-:
Edward P. Cheyney introduces England's working past in An Introduction to the Industrial and Social History of England, issued in 1901. The British Isles, he begins, lie northwest of Europe, split from it by the Channel and North Sea. At the narrowest the gap is only twenty miles.

Cheyney traces farming, towns, guilds, and trade from early times onward. A picture of Gidea Hall in Essex shows a new manor amid open fields. The book aimed at students meeting economic history as a set subject. Its clear, plain survey helped fix that subject in schools on both sides of the Atlantic.
50791-the-angevins-and-the-charter-1154-:
S M Toyne wrote The Angevins and the Charter for Bell's English History Source Books. Toyne was headmaster of St Peter's School at York. The book came out in London in 1913.

The years run from 1154 to 1216, the age of the first Plantagenet kings. Toyne treats the start of English law in that age. He also covers the invasion of Ireland and the Crusades. The book is built from source extracts, not mere summary. Passages from Jocelin de Brakelond and the Song of Dermot appear by kind leave. Students get the words of the time itself. The charter of the title is the great charter won from King John.
6134-the-evolution-of-an-empire-a-brief-:
Mary Parmele asks readers to bear in mind the difficulty of painting a very large picture, with multitudinous characters and details, upon a very small canvas. Her brief sketch of England traces to their sources currents entering English life today, and starting points of threads legislative, judicial, and social.

Two things, she argues, intertwine most closely with England's life: religion and money have been the great evolutionary factors. Resistance to money extortions by rulers, and violation of religious instincts, made nearly all that is vital in English history. Parmele compresses centuries into a readable strand.
78511-a-comparison-between-the-british-s:
A Comparison Between the British Sugar Colonies and New England is an anonymous pamphlet on colonial trade. James Roberts printed it in London in 1732, priced at sixpence. A letter to a Member of Parliament is added at the end.

The writer argues from the Custom-house books and from evidence laid before the House of Commons. Exports of woollen and other English manufactures to the British sugar colonies, he says, are vastly greater than those to New England. Imports from the sugar colonies into England are likewise far greater. His task, he declares, is to prove that the advantage of the sugar colonies to Great Britain must be perpetual, if they are encouraged and protected. The pamphlet is a salvo in the pamphlet war that preceded the Molasses Act, defending the West India interest against New England's trade.
doe-osti-3005899-particle-dynamics-in-th:
Uwe R. Kortshagen and Christopher J. Hogan of the University of Minnesota give the final report for DOE project DE-SC0022242, dated November 30, 2025. The subject is dusty plasmas in their afterglow: what happens to dust particles in the seconds after a plasma switches off. Most dusty plasma research studies the steady, driven state. The decaying state, which every industrial plasma passes through, was comparatively unmapped.

The distinction matters commercially. In semiconductor processing, particles only a few nanometers across can ruin a wafer, and they form and move during exactly these transients. In space, comet tails and planetary rings present natural versions of the same physics. The project combined experiment, materials chemistry, and simulation. Personnel notes trace a postdoc's move to a faculty post in Eindhoven and a doctoral student's experimental campaign.
doe-osti-3024527-hydrogen-education-for-:
Electric Power Research Institute ran the H2EDGE project, Hydrogen Education for a Decarbonized Global Economy, under award DE-EE0009253 from October 2020 to September 2025. Eladio Knipping managed the program, with Oregon State University, the University of Delaware, the University of Houston, and GTI Energy as partners. Krystal Rose York and Ashley Roberts are the report's named authors. A hydrogen workforce cannot grow faster than the courses that train it.

One strand audited what universities actually teach. A matrix of specialized hydrogen courses across the 25 largest universities for 2023-2024 sorts offerings into 12 categories and marks the gaps in white. Five of the 25, twenty percent, offered more than 100 hydrogen-specific courses, and four taught across all 12 categories, while other named schools sat below the full sample average.
the-evolution-of-an-empire-a-brief-histo:
Mary Parmele's The Evolution of an Empire gives a brief sketch of English history. Her preface owns the hard task: a vast picture with crowds of figures must fit a small canvas. She aims to trace the streams that feed England's life today, and to mark where its laws, courts, and customs began. Two threads, she says, weave through all: religion and money.

Kings taxed, folk resisted, and faith shifted power. Parmele wrote many such short histories for home study. Her clear thread makes a first map of England's growth from Saxon roots to her own close of century.
the-evolution-of-dodd-a-pedagogical-stor:
William Hawley Smith's The Evolution of Dodd, dated by its title page to 1897, calls itself a pedagogical story of the survival of the fittest. Its mottoes hold that social forms are made for man, not man for them, and that creation's chief aim is the growth of the single soul. Chapter one opens with joy in the Weaver house at the birth of a boy, the first of his line.

A father feels his manhood sealed by the word father. Dodd's schooling, scrapes, and slow making fill the tale. Smith, a school man, argues that boys grow by nature, not by moulds.
